Converting a Maitland lawn to synthetic turf

A residential lawn conversion in Maitland runs $8–$18 per square foot installed as of September 2026, most jobs between $10–$16. The city's own Land Development Code, rewritten in October 2024, still doesn't name synthetic turf, which leaves the state's May 2026 standard as the operative rule for most of what a crew runs into here.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

A rewritten code that skipped turf entirely

Maitland's Community Development Department reviews exterior work under a Land Development Code recodified from the ground up in October 2024, and a search of that current code turns up no section addressing synthetic or artificial turf specifically. That's a different situation from a city that once had an old turf rule and is now squaring it against the state standard; Maitland's rulebook simply never wrote one, so a residential conversion here answers to Rule 62-308.100 directly, plus whatever ordinary drainage or grading review the city applies to any exterior alteration.

Why the base still has to drain faster than the storm

Perforated turf backing on its own passes water at more than thirty inches an hour, but that number means little if the base underneath can't move water at a similar rate. A Central Florida cell can drop one to three inches of rain in under an hour during a typical Maitland summer, and a base compacted too tight, or built from unwashed fill that's crusted over, can't keep up with that pace even though the turf on top clearly can. When a new lawn puddles after a storm, the base is almost always the reason, not a defect in the turf itself.

Mid-century lots built for bigger yards

Homes going up through the 1970s and into the 1980s here tended toward larger lots than the infill built more recently in parts of Winter Springs or Casselberry, which usually means more open lawn to work with and fewer of the narrow side-yard constraints that shape a job in an older, denser town. What that older construction can carry instead is decades of landscaping changes and buried irrigation zones from past owners, which a crew has to map before excavation starts rather than assume from the current layout.

Choosing a backing that actually drains

Every residential turf product we install uses a perforated backing built to pass water at well over thirty inches an hour, since a backing that seals up under a Central Florida storm defeats the point of a base built to drain. Two backing styles come up most on a Maitland lawn: a lighter perforated polyurethane for a budget-first job, and a heavier, fully permeable, double-stitched version for a full-sun front lawn under years of foot traffic. Both meet the same drainage requirement; the difference is how much infill weight and stitching the backing can carry over a decade of afternoon rain before it starts to sag or stretch at the seams.

A 1970s ranch home near Lake Sybelia

Say you have a 540 sq ft backyard behind a 1976 ranch home two streets from Lake Sybelia, flat and open with an old irrigation zone running through the middle of it that the current owner inherited from the house's original build. At $10–$16 per square foot, that lawn prices around $5,400 to $8,640 installed, with capping the buried zone's heads a small add rather than a separate project.

A similar-sized yard near Altamonte Springs or Longwood prices the same way; what changes the bid here is whatever the old irrigation layout adds to the prep work, not the town's name.

Trimming turf at a driveway or patio edge

Once the base is feathered to meet an existing driveway or patio on a Maitland lot, turf gets rolled across that boundary and trimmed tight to the hardscape edge as one of the last steps, after seams are set but before final infill goes in. That edge typically takes an adhesive-set bond rather than nails, since there's no soil at that specific point to anchor into, unlike the rest of the lawn's perimeter. Getting the trim line clean here matters more than elsewhere, since a driveway edge is one of the most visible and heavily walked transitions on the whole property.

Why a lawn can't cross a swale or hug a pond

Two setbacks apply to any Maitland lawn near water: turf has to stay at least ten feet from a natural or man-made waterbody unless a seawall or bulkhead already separates the two, and it can never go inside a drainage swale, ditch, or a stormwater pond's littoral zone, no matter how flat and convenient that strip of ground looks. Both rules exist because turf and the base under it change how water moves across a lot, and a swale or pond edge is specifically where the state doesn't want that changed. A yard backing onto a retention pond usually has more usable space than these setbacks first suggest, just not right up to the water's edge.

The same ridge soil, a different water source

Candler and Apopka series sand sits under most of Maitland the same way it does under Winter Park, draining fast on its own but still needing a washed crushed-rock base to hold the surface level. Because Maitland runs its own water utility instead of buying through OUC or a county system, capping the in-ground heads under a new lawn is a step the city's own Water Production and Distribution division can confirm directly, rather than routing the question through a regional provider.

Walking the perimeter after a Maitland storm

After a tropical storm or a stretch of unusually hard rain, walking the full perimeter of a lawn is worth the ten minutes it takes, checking specifically for a corner or edge that's lifted where it was nailed or bordered. Wind and standing water are exactly what the state's anchoring rule is meant to withstand, so a lifted edge after a storm usually means that spot needs attention, not that the whole install failed. Catching it early on a Maitland property, while it's still a small section, keeps the fix to a quick re-anchor instead of a larger repair once more water or foot traffic works the gap wider.

Questions people ask

Since Maitland's code doesn't mention turf, is a permit still required?

Ordinary building and land-alteration permitting still applies to exterior work even without a turf-specific rule, and capping irrigation heads can need its own plumbing permit. Confirm the current requirement for a specific scope with Community Development at (407) 539-6150.

Do older Maitland lots near Martin Marietta-era subdivisions have unusual soil to plan around?

Not unusually so. The same Candler and Apopka ridge sand common across this part of Orange County sits under most of the city's mid-century subdivisions, and the base build doesn't change based on when a lot was platted.
